name: Tithonus Toll

detectability.signature: Fleet-sync pings return stretched or compressed; clock-skew maps trace the field's breathing edges

proximity: Chronometers drift seconds against fleet sync, then snap back
Voice comms take on a smeared, doubled quality
contact: Crew report hours passing outside that felt like minutes aboard
Departure timestamps refuse to reconcile with arrival records
prolonged_exposure: Cumulative aging gap opening between crew and the outside universe
Desynchronization deep enough to strand crews years from their own era

phenomena: Radio signals occasionally arriving before they are sent
Ships exiting older or newer than their logs claim
Biological matter aging unevenly across a single deck
hazards: Crew aging and de-aging relative to standard time
opportunities: Unique research opportunity into reversible aging
Recovery of lost ships whose crews may still be alive inside the gradient
known_incidents: The tug Anabasis drifted the field for six days and returned with a crew eleven months older and one member younger
Insurance boards now void coverage for any vessel lingering past the second gradient
description: Nothing marks the Toll's boundary; space looks ordinary in every direction, which is the trap. Only time misbehaves here, pooling in gradients that breathe across a volume wider than most planets. Fleet-sync pings return subtly wrong, and seasoned spacers trust that wrongness more than any chart.

The field pulses on a rough nine-hour rhythm, its steepness shifting enough that no two crossings cost the same. A cautious transit might shave minutes from a crew's lives; a careless one can collect decades. Ships have come out carrying crews visibly older than their own captains, and once, famously, younger.

The anomaly takes its name from the first recorded casualty, a navigator who entered middle-aged and left white-haired while his ship logged only hours. Who or what set the gradient breathing remains open argument; the field shows no natural anatomy and no machine seam. It simply collects its due from anyone who lingers.

Research buoys now stitch the boundary with synchronized clocks, mapping each pulse as it arrives. Rescue syndicates advertise retrieval services for vessels stranded deep in the gradient, priced accordingly. Transit is legal, survivable, and never quite free.
